title: MindFlow: Mind Supernet Powered Thinking Flows for Research Idea Innovation
one_liner: Treat idea generation as a search over many composable reasoning flows so that a controller can learn which sequences of thinking steps produce ideas that are new, plausible, and feasible.
lead: This paper studies scientific idea generation as a controllable search problem rather than as a single prompt. A good research idea must balance several goals at once: it should be fresh enough to matter, grounded enough to make sense, and concrete enough to be testable. Static pipelines struggle because the same fixed order of steps does not suit every topic. MindFlow builds a large space of possible reasoning flows from modular operators, samples candidate flows for a topic, and updates the controller toward flows that win relative comparisons, so that the system gradually favors more effective patterns of thought.

problem.h2: Why fixed ideation pipelines fall short
paras: Research ideation is open-ended. Different topics may need different reasoning orders: one topic may benefit from finding a neglected problem first, while another may benefit from combining methods from two areas.

A fixed prompt or static multi-step pipeline can produce some good ideas, but it cannot adapt its thinking pattern to the topic. The paper asks whether the system can search over many possible reasoning flows and learn which ones work best.

callout.b: The paper's move in one sentence.
callout.html: Represent ideation as a flexible graph of thinking operators, then learn which sampled flows produce better ideas because repeated comparison reveals which flows balance freshness, plausibility, and feasibility more reliably.

panels.title: 1. Topic arrives
panels.viz_args: Example topic: improve scientific discovery in biology
panels.caption: A single topic can be explored in many different ways because there are many possible problem and solution paths.

panels.title: 2. Static workflow is too rigid
panels.viz_args: Always brainstorm, then filter, then write
panels.caption: One fixed order can miss opportunities because some topics need a different sequence of thinking steps.

panels.title: 3. MindFlow samples a reasoning flow
panels.viz_args: Find problem -> check evidence -> combine methods -> stress-test
panels.caption: The controller selects a flow from a large library of operators.

panels.title: 4. Candidate ideas compete
panels.viz_args: Compare ideas by quality, plausibility, and feasibility
panels.caption: Relative ranking guides learning because open-ended quality is easier to compare than to score absolutely.

panels.title: 5. Better flows are reused
panels.caption: The controller shifts toward stronger thinking flows so that later ideas improve.

steps.text: Define reusable thinking steps such as finding a gap, combining areas, checking evidence, or testing feasibility.
Allow many possible graph-shaped combinations so that different topics can follow different reasoning paths.

steps.b: Sample a flow for a topic
steps.text: Use a controller to choose one candidate flow because the search space is too large to test exhaustively.
Run the sampled flow, then rank ideas in tournaments so that stronger flows receive more support.
Increase the chance of choosing successful flows so that future topics are explored with better reasoning patterns.

paras: The paper changes idea generation from one fixed chain of prompts into a learned policy over many possible reasoning flows.
object.object: Choice of thinking flow for ideation

hidden.name: Quality of a reasoning flow for a given topic
paras: The key hidden quantity is whether a particular sequence of thinking operators is well suited to the current topic. You can observe the final idea, but you do not know in advance which flow will best balance freshness, plausibility, and feasibility.

MindFlow estimates this hidden quantity indirectly through repeated competitions among candidate ideas. A flow is treated as better when the ideas it produces win more often because those wins indicate that the underlying reasoning path is productive.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark operator types that often determine whether a flow yields a strong idea.

reads.html: The hidden quantity is whether this pattern of thinking is a good way to generate ideas for this topic.
The controller learns a topic-conditioned pattern of preference over graph-shaped reasoning flows by observing which flows yield stronger ideas in comparative evaluation.

mechanism.h2: Why this works: the system can search over reasoning patterns instead of assuming one pattern fits all topics
paras: Static ideation pipelines bake in one view of how ideas should emerge. That works only when the fixed order happens to match the topic. A supernet of operators works better because it allows the system to try many different reasoning paths and keep the ones that repeatedly produce stronger outcomes.

Relative ranking is also important. Open-ended idea quality is difficult to score on an absolute scale, but people and models can often judge which of two candidate ideas is better. That gives the controller a usable learning signal because winning flows can be favored even when exact numeric scores are unreliable.

stages.s: Better future flow choices because winning flows are favored

math.words: A compact view is to give each flow a higher value when the ideas produced by that flow win pairwise or tournament comparisons more often, while reducing the value of flows that repeatedly produce weak or impractical ideas.
symbols: overall desirability of using reasoning flow f for future topics
how often ideas from flow f beat competing ideas in relative ranking
how well the flow tends to satisfy the desired balance of freshness, plausibility, and feasibility
how often the flow produces weak, unrealistic, or poorly grounded ideas

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Flow A: find a problem gap, combine two methods, then run a feasibility check.
Flow B: brainstorm freely, then write the first idea directly.
Suppose Flow A wins 7 of 10 comparisons and usually produces grounded ideas.
Suppose Flow B wins 3 of 10 comparisons and often skips feasibility.
Flow A receives the higher value because its operator order produces ideas that judges prefer more often.

math.note: The paper uses a probabilistic supernet and tournament-based optimization rather than this exact formula, but the formula captures the selection pressure.

charts.title: Static ideation workflow
charts.note: A fixed workflow helps somewhat, but it cannot adapt its reasoning order to the topic because every topic is forced through the same sequence of steps.

charts.title: MindFlow
charts.note: The paper reports stronger idea generation across diverse topics because the controller can choose and improve reasoning flows instead of reusing one rigid path.

items.b: The operator library may be incomplete.
items.html: If the system lacks an operator needed for a topic, the controller cannot discover the best flow because the right reasoning step is absent from the search space.

items.b: Relative ranking may favor polished but shallow ideas.
items.html: Comparisons can be misled if judges overvalue presentation, so the evaluation protocol must inspect substance as well as surface quality.
Sampling many flows and evaluating many ideas takes time, so practical use may require pruning weak flows early.
The paper is useful because it treats ideation as a learnable search over reasoning patterns rather than a single handcrafted prompt.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a small idea-generation system with eight to ten thinking operators. Give it several research topics and allow the controller to sample different operator sequences for each one so that the demo can test whether topic-specific flow choices matter. For every topic, generate several candidate ideas and compare them with a judging routine that checks problem quality, solution quality, and feasibility.

The demo should show that the controller gradually prefers some flows over others because those flows win more comparisons. It should also show topic variation, where one topic benefits from a gap-finding-first flow while another benefits from an evidence-first flow.
demo.closing: The demo must prove that learning which reasoning flow to use can improve research ideation beyond a fixed workflow because different topics benefit from different sequences of thinking steps.
